title: The Skeletal System
intro: Connect bone structure with support, movement, mineral balance, growth, repair, and development. Distinguish the skeleton's regions, joint types, and the two main routes of bone formation.

sections.title: Bone tissue and long-bone structure

steps.title: Bone is living connective tissue
bullets: Bone contains living cells embedded in a mineralized extracellular matrix. Collagen contributes flexibility and tensile strength; mineral salts make the matrix rigid and resistant to compression.
A long bone has a shaft called the **diaphysis** and expanded ends called **epiphyses**. The periosteum covers its external surface except at articular regions.
Compact bone forms a dense outer region, while spongy bone contains a lattice of trabeculae. The spaces within spongy bone can contain marrow.

steps.title: Bone-cell roles are distinct
bullets: **Osteoblasts** build bone by secreting osteoid and supporting its mineralization.
**Osteoclasts** resorb bone, while **osteocytes** are mature cells that help maintain the matrix and sense mechanical conditions.
Bone also stores minerals, protects organs, provides attachment sites for muscles, and houses marrow involved in blood-cell production.

steps.title: Cartilage and ligaments are different tissues
bullets: Cartilage supports and cushions structures; articular cartilage reduces friction where bones meet.
Ligaments connect bone to bone and help stabilize joints. They are not the same as tendons, which connect muscle to bone.

steps.title: Additional course details: bone composition, cells, and supporting tissues
bullets: Bone consists of calcium-phosphate crystals in extracellular matrix together with living cells, nerves, and blood vessels. Compact bone forms the shaft and outer ends; the diaphysis holds yellow, fat-rich marrow, while trabeculae fill the inner epiphyses and contain red marrow with hematopoietic stem cells.

Osteoblasts in the periosteum secrete mostly collagen osteoid and enzymes that crystallize calcium phosphate. Osteoclasts degrade bone. Osteocytes are embedded osteoblasts in lacunae within osteons and receive nutrients from vessels in central canals.

Ligaments are dense fibrous connective tissue with aligned collagen and fibroblasts. Cartilage contains collagen and elastic fibres in a gel-like matrix: fibrocartilage makes knee menisci and intervertebral discs; hyaline cartilage covers joint ends; elastic cartilage forms the outer ear and epiglottis.

boxes.text: Bone combines a tough collagen framework with mineral reinforcement, allowing it to resist forces while remaining a living tissue that can adapt.
Osteoblasts build; osteoclasts resorb; osteocytes maintain and sense.
Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone. Do not use the terms interchangeably.

sections.title: Bone remodeling and fracture repair

steps.title: Remodeling responds to the body
bullets: Bone is continually resorbed and replaced. Osteoclasts and osteoblasts coordinate the removal and deposition of matrix.
Mechanical loading influences where bone is maintained or added. Calcium needs and hormonal signals also affect remodeling.
Remodeling is not the same as growth in bone length: it renews and reshapes existing tissue.

steps.title: A fracture heals in stages
bullets: Damage to blood vessels forms a fracture hematoma. Inflammatory and repair cells then enter the injured region.
A soft callus bridges the fracture before a harder bony callus develops. Remodeling gradually reshapes the new bone.
The sequence depends on adequate blood supply and stabilization; a fracture does not immediately return to its original structure.

steps.title: Additional course details: loading, minerals, hormones, and repair
bullets: Bone remodeling responds to mechanical stress and circulating Ca?? needs. When blood Ca?? is low, bone is resorbed; osteoclast enzymes dissolve matrix and Ca?? and phosphate are released to blood. Removal stimulates osteoblasts to deposit new osteoid.

High compressive stress increases osteoblast deposition; low-compression regions experience resorption and comparatively less osteoblast activity. The course deck identifies parathyroid hormone as stimulating osteoclast activity and calcitonin as stimulating osteoblast activity.

After fracture, a hematoma forms. Bone-marrow mesenchymal stem cells become fibroblasts and chondroblasts that make a fibrocartilage callus; osteoclasts clear dead tissue and clot remnants; periosteal osteoblasts deposit osteoid that mineralizes. Repair takes weeks to months and the healed region is often thicker and stronger.

sections.title: Axial and appendicular skeleton

steps.title: The axial skeleton forms the central framework
bullets: The axial skeleton includes the skull, vertebral column, ribs, and sternum. It supports the body axis and protects the brain, spinal cord, heart, and lungs.
The vertebral column has cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal regions. There are seven cervical, twelve thoracic, and five lumbar vertebrae.
The rib cage includes twelve pairs of ribs. The first seven pairs attach directly to the sternum; the lower rib groups have indirect or no anterior attachment.

steps.title: The appendicular skeleton supports movement
bullets: The appendicular skeleton includes the pectoral and pelvic girdles and the bones of the upper and lower limbs.
The pectoral girdle includes the clavicle and scapula. The pelvic girdle transfers upper-body weight to the lower limbs.
Bone names and landmarks help identify where muscles attach, how joints move, and which structures protect nearby organs.

steps.title: Skull and specialized bones
bullets: Cranial bones enclose the brain; facial bones support the face and sensory structures.
The hyoid is unusual because it does not articulate directly with another bone. It provides attachment for muscles of the tongue and throat.
The small auditory ossicles transmit vibrations through the middle ear.

steps.title: Additional course details: named bones and counts
bullets: The typical skeleton has 206 bones: long bones (limbs and digits), short bones (wrists and ankles), flat bones (cranium, sternum, ribs), irregular bones (hip bones and vertebrae), and sesamoid bones (patella).

Cranial bones: frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid. Facial bones: maxilla, palatine, vomer, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, mandible. Skull foramina transmit cranial nerves, spinal cord, and vessels. The hyoid does not articulate with another bone and anchors tongue, larynx, and pharynx muscles; malleus, incus, and stapes transmit eardrum vibrations to the inner ear.

Vertebral counts are 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, and 4 fused coccygeal. Twelve rib pairs protect heart and lungs; the upper ten connect to sternum through cartilage, while the lower two are floating ribs.

The pectoral girdle is clavicle and scapula; forelimb: humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges, with opposable thumbs. The pelvic girdle includes sacrum and coxal bones; hindlimb: femur, patella, tibia, fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges.

boxes.text: The axial skeleton prioritizes support and protection, while the appendicular skeleton connects limbs to the trunk and enables a wide range of movement.
Axial = central axis. Appendicular = girdles and limbs.
The sacrum belongs to the axial vertebral column; the pelvic girdle also includes the coxal bones.

sections.title: Joint structure and movement

steps.title: Classify joints by structure and motion
bullets: A joint, or articulation, is a location where bones meet. Structural classes include fibrous, cartilaginous, and synovial joints.
Fibrous joints generally allow little movement; cartilaginous joints allow limited movement; synovial joints are freely movable.
Functional classifications describe how much movement a joint permits. Structural type and functional movement are related but are not the same classification.

steps.title: Synovial joints share key structures
bullets: A joint capsule surrounds the synovial cavity. Its inner synovial membrane produces fluid that lubricates and helps nourish the joint surfaces.
Articular cartilage covers the ends of bones, reducing friction and distributing forces.
Ligaments reinforce a joint and limit excessive movement; the shape of the articulating surfaces also affects the permitted motion.

steps.title: Additional course details: articulation types and movement
bullets: Fibrous joints are immovable (cranial fontanels harden into sutures); cartilaginous joints are slightly movable (including vertebral joints); synovial joints are freely movable and have a fluid-filled capsule with ligaments attaching the bones.

The synovial membrane lines the capsule and secretes cushioning, lubricating fluid; hyaline cartilage covers the articulating surfaces. Hinge joints move in one plane (knee, elbow), while ball-and-socket joints move in all planes (hip, shoulder).

boxes.text: A fluid-filled cavity and lubricated cartilage permit low-friction movement while the capsule and ligaments help maintain joint stability.
Synovial: capsule, cavity, synovial fluid, and articular cartilage.
A freely movable joint is not an unsupported joint: its capsule, ligaments, muscles, and tendons contribute to stability.

sections.title: Bone formation and growth

steps.title: Two routes form bone
bullets: **Intramembranous ossification** forms bone directly as mesenchymal cells differentiate into osteoblasts and deposit osteoid.
**Endochondral ossification** begins with a cartilage model that is gradually replaced by bone. Many limb bones form through this route.
These terms describe how bone forms, not which embryonic region the precursor tissue came from.

steps.title: Growth plates lengthen long bones
bullets: At an epiphyseal growth plate, cartilage cells divide and enlarge while bone is deposited on the shaft-facing side.
When the growth plate closes, lengthwise growth at that site stops; bones can still remodel.
Hormones regulate growth and maturation. Growth hormone supports childhood growth, while sex hormones contribute to the adolescent growth spurt and eventual plate closure.

steps.title: Bone growth is regulated
bullets: Long-bone lengthening requires an active growth plate. Abnormalities that disrupt cartilage-cell development can alter growth.
Bone diameter can increase through deposition at the outer surface even as internal bone is remodeled.

steps.title: Additional course details: formation, growth, hormones, and achondroplasia
bullets: Endochondral ossification begins with a hyaline-cartilage model: chondroblasts/chondrocytes form the model, chondrocytes degenerate, fetal osteoblasts migrate in, and bone replaces cartilage. The primary ossification centre forms in the fetus; secondary centres form in childhood.

Growth plates contain actively dividing chondrocytes and bone deposition. Chondrocyte division lengthens bone; their cartilage is replaced by bone. Growth ceases when the plate closes and all its cartilage becomes bone. Intramembranous ossification starts when mesenchymal stem cells become osteoblasts; osteoid spicules fuse into trabeculae, and osteoblasts trapped in matrix become osteocytes.

Growth hormone stimulates childhood lengthening; estrogen and testosterone promote early-adolescent lengthening and later growth-plate replacement and closure. Adult bone shape and thickness remain responsive to parathyroid hormone, calcitonin, fracture repair, and compression.

Achondroplasia (about 1 in 20,000 births) is usually autosomal dominant and associated with an activating FGFR3 mutation. Persistent receptor activity stops chondrocyte division, impairing growth, especially in long bones.

boxes.text: A cartilage model permits the developing long bone to grow in length before the growth plate closes and the bone reaches maturity.
Intramembranous: bone directly from mesenchyme. Endochondral: bone replaces cartilage.
Embryonic origin and ossification route are separate questions; a tissue's source does not by itself determine which formation process it uses.

sections.title: Embryonic origins of the skeleton

steps.title: Different regions contribute different bones
bullets: Much of the axial skeleton below the skull develops from somites derived from paraxial mesoderm. The sclerotome contributes to vertebrae and ribs.
The appendicular skeleton develops largely from somatic lateral plate mesoderm and the limb buds.
Cranial neural crest contributes many facial bones, auditory ossicles, and the hyoid.

steps.title: Regional identity is patterned
bullets: Vertebrae acquire different regional identities along the head-to-tail axis. Hox gene expression contributes to this positional pattern.
Somite derivatives include more than bone: sclerotome forms skeletal components, while adjacent somite regions contribute muscle and other tissues.
A bone's embryonic origin is not identical to its adult structural classification or its route of ossification.

steps.title: Additional course details: embryonic origin and patterning
bullets: Axial skeleton below the skull largely derives from somite sclerotome and the notochord; appendicular skeleton derives largely from somatic lateral-plate mesoderm. Facial bones, hyoid, and ossicles derive from cranial neural crest.

Sclerotome forms ribs and vertebrae; its central arthrotome contributes to vertebral joints and parts of ribs. Most intervertebral-disc tissue derives from notochord. Limb-bone precursors migrate into limb buds; a reaction-diffusion (Turing-model) framework describes sequential limb-skeleton patterning.
HOX spatial collinearity links gene order to position: 3? HOX genes are expressed more anteriorly, 5? genes more posteriorly. HOX patterns establish vertebral identity and differ among species.

Embryonic origin is not the same as ossification route: most neural-crest skull bones are intramembranous, but neural-crest-derived ossicles and hyoid are endochondral; the paraxial-mesoderm-derived parietal bone is intramembranous. Pharyngeal arch 1 forms facial bones and mandible; arches 1 and 2 form ossicles; arches 2 and 3 form hyoid.

boxes.text: Regional patterning coordinates bones, muscles, and joints so that structures form in the right place and connect appropriately.
Somites contribute axial structures; lateral plate mesoderm contributes limb skeleton; cranial neural crest contributes many facial structures.
Do not confuse where a bone's precursor cells originate with whether that bone forms by intramembranous or endochondral ossification.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. Osteoblasts secrete osteoid. II. Osteoclasts deposit most new bone matrix. III. Osteocytes help maintain mature bone.
quiz.why: Osteoblasts form osteoid, and osteocytes maintain mature bone. Osteoclasts resorb rather than deposit bone.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. Collagen contributes tensile strength to bone. II. Mineral salts contribute rigidity. III. Bone matrix is entirely nonliving.
quiz.why: Collagen and mineral contribute different mechanical properties, and bone also contains living cells.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. The diaphysis is the shaft of a long bone. II. The epiphyses are its expanded ends. III. The periosteum covers the articular surfaces.
quiz.why: The diaphysis is the shaft and epiphyses are the ends; articular regions are not covered by periosteum.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. A ligament normally joins bone to bone. II. A tendon normally joins muscle to bone. III. Both terms describe the same attachment.
quiz.why: Ligaments connect bones; tendons connect muscle and bone.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. The axial skeleton includes the vertebral column. II. The appendicular skeleton includes the pectoral girdle. III. The pelvic girdle is part of the axial skeleton.
quiz.why: The axial skeleton includes the vertebral column; both limb girdles belong to the appendicular skeleton.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. The rib cage protects organs in the thorax. II. Humans typically have twelve pairs of ribs. III. Every rib attaches directly to the sternum.
quiz.why: There are twelve rib pairs, but only the upper seven pairs attach directly to the sternum.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. The hyoid directly articulates with the mandible. II. The hyoid provides muscle attachment in the throat. III. Auditory ossicles transmit vibrations in the middle ear.
quiz.why: The hyoid does not articulate directly with another bone; it anchors muscles. Ossicles transmit sound vibrations.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. The vertebral column has five anatomical regions. II. Thoracic vertebrae are associated with ribs. III. The cervical region contains twelve vertebrae.
quiz.why: The column has five regions and twelve thoracic vertebrae; the cervical region has seven.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. Fibrous joints generally allow little movement. II. Cartilaginous joints permit limited movement. III. Synovial joints lack a joint cavity.
quiz.why: Synovial joints have a cavity enclosed by a capsule.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. Synovial fluid reduces friction. II. Articular cartilage covers bone ends at a synovial joint. III. Ligaments reinforce joints.
quiz.why: Synovial fluid, articular cartilage, and ligaments each contribute to joint function and stability.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. Intramembranous ossification uses a cartilage model. II. Endochondral ossification replaces cartilage. III. Both processes produce bone tissue.
quiz.why: Endochondral ossification replaces cartilage, while intramembranous ossification forms bone directly from mesenchymal tissue.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. Long bones lengthen at growth plates. II. Growth plates contain cartilage. III. Longitudinal growth continues at a site after its plate has closed.
quiz.why: Closure of the growth plate ends lengthwise growth at that location, although remodeling continues.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. The fracture sequence begins with a hematoma. II. A soft callus precedes a hard callus. III. Remodeling is the first event after a fracture.
quiz.why: The early hematoma is followed by callus formation; remodeling occurs later.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. Mechanical loading can influence bone remodeling. II. Osteoclasts remove bone matrix. III. Remodeling and lengthwise growth are identical processes.
quiz.why: Remodeling renews and reshapes bone, whereas lengthwise growth depends on growth plates.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. The sclerotome contributes to vertebrae and ribs. II. Somites derive from paraxial mesoderm. III. Every skull bone derives from a somite.
quiz.why: Many skull structures have other embryonic sources, including cranial neural crest.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. The limb skeleton develops largely from lateral plate mesoderm. II. Many facial bones receive cranial neural crest contributions. III. Bone embryonic origin identifies its ossification method without exception.
quiz.why: Embryonic origin and the process by which bone forms are separate characteristics.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. Hox gene expression contributes to regional identity along the body axis. II. Vertebrae differ in features by region. III. All vertebrae are structurally identical.
quiz.why: Regional patterning produces vertebrae with different features, such as the association of thoracic vertebrae with ribs.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. Compact bone is dense tissue. II. Spongy bone contains trabeculae. III. The spaces in spongy bone can contain marrow.
quiz.why: All three statements describe features of compact and spongy bone.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. Bone protects organs. II. Bone provides muscle attachment. III. Bone contributes to mineral storage.
quiz.why: Bone supports protection, movement, and mineral homeostasis.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. Osteoclasts resorb tissue. II. Osteoblasts secrete osteoid. III. Osteocytes are mature cells embedded in bone.
quiz.why: Each cell type has a distinct role in the living bone tissue.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. The synovial membrane lines the inner capsule. II. Synovial fluid helps lubricate the joint. III. Articular cartilage is a ligament.
quiz.why: Articular cartilage is cartilage covering bone ends; it is not a ligament.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. A tendon joins muscle to bone. II. A ligament joins bone to bone. III. Both structures can contribute to movement or joint stability.
quiz.why: Tendons transmit muscle force to bone, while ligaments connect bones and help stabilize joints.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. Growth hormone supports bone growth during childhood. II. Sex hormones contribute to adolescent growth and growth-plate closure. III. Bone lengthening occurs at the outer periosteum.
quiz.why: Longitudinal growth occurs at growth plates; outer-surface deposition can increase bone diameter.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are true? I. The pelvic girdle helps transfer upper-body weight to the lower limbs. II. The pectoral girdle includes clavicles and scapulae. III. The sacrum is an appendicular bone.
quiz.why: The sacrum is part of the axial vertebral column; the pelvic girdle includes coxal bones.
